newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO to hold U.S.-sponsored security talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO to hold U.S.-sponsored security talks.

text.p: Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials will hold talks on Sunday as part of a trilateral framework set by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, a senior PLO official said.
Mohammad Dahlan, chief of the Palestinian Preventive Security agency in the Gaza Strip, told Reuters the meeting would be held in the self-ruled West Bank city of Ramallah.
Ross spent four days in the region last week, arranging Israel-PLO security talks attended by U.S. representatives in the aftermath of a double suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market on July 30.

He was also preparing the ground for a visit to the Middle East planned for September by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. She has demanded improved Israeli-Palestinian security cooperation before she makes her maiden trip to the region.

In a sign of a slight easing of tensions, Israeli government sources said on Sunday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent a personal envoy to thank Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat for PLO aid in finding the killers of an Israeli taxi driver.
They said the envoy, Yitzhak Molho, secretly met the Palestinian president in Gaza on Saturday night.
The sources said the men also discussed Ross's visit and sanctions Israel imposed on Palestinians after the two suicide bombers killed 14 people in a Jerusalem market.
There was no immediate indication of any easing of the sanctions following Saturday's meeting.

Israel demanded Arafat arrest militants and crush the infrastructure of Islamist groups after the suicide attacks. It also sealed off Palestinian areas and froze millions of dollars of financial transfers it owes the Palestinian Authority (PA).
Washington has also repeatedly condemned Israel's sanctions as "counterproductive" and "unhelpful". The PA has said it will match the sanctions with a partial boycott on Israeli goods.
The Palestinian president rejected on Sunday Israeli allegations that his planned "national unity" talks with militant groups amounted to "appeasement of terrorism".
"No doubt we are against terrorist activities...but this is a Palestinian interest and we are insisting to carry on dialogue with all Palestinian groups," Arafat told reporters in Gaza.
"We are as Palestinians completely committed to the peace process and at the same time we are facing collective punishment from the Israeli government," Arafat said.
Arafat said on Saturday he would not bow to Israeli "dictates" he clamp down on militants and called for the "national unity" talks this week with all Palestinian groups.

The Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas, which Israeli security sources had a hand in July's attack, took part in a first round of unity talks in February. Hamas boycotted a later round in April, saying its activists remained in Arafat's jails.
Arafat on Saturday cited the arrest by his forces of three Palestinian car thieves who confessed to murdering an Israeli taxi driver in Jericho as proof that the PA was working with Israeli police.

Israeli police praised Palestinian forces for apprehending the driver's killers, who received long prison terms in a summary trial, but Israeli officials said cooperation in a criminal case could not replace a crackdown on "terror".
A Netanyahu aide on Saturday criticised Arafat's outreaching to militant groups.

"(Arafat) has been making agreements that flirt with the terrorist organisations since the Palestinian Authority was established. We don't believe that this kind of appeasement of terrorism works," aide David Bar-Illan said.
The Palestinian Authority says it is making "100 percent effort" on security but refuses to take orders from Israel.
Netanyahu insists he will ease the sanctions hand-in-hand with Palestinian measures against militants.
